doc.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

chapter: Studio philosophy: making the artist comfortable
title: Carole King and the rhythm section in her living room
summary: Hank sets Carole King at a piano with the band around her so it felt like her living room, and criticizes putting players in separate rooms.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: to look in the booth when there’s people in there. I don’t like to see the lights on.” I always worked with my lights down low once I got the balance I needed and that was it. People would look at me and say, “Gee are you guys in the booth?” “Yeah.” My thing was you get it as comfortable out there. For example with Carole King, Carole liked to work, because she was a musician, she liked to work with the band. So I had to set up those dates with a piano in the middle of the room and Carole would be there, and surround her with the band, be it a couple of guitars, the drummer, I just set them up so — the only way I could describe it is they were sitting in Carole’s living room. The more comfortable it is out there, the most comfortable their hearing is, their earphones are right, the balance is right, the room feels — all those things are part of making a good record. You know I’ve seen guys put everybody in a booth. Two guitars are in one booth and the guys on the other side of the room are in another room, the artist is in another booth. They don’t even see each other. That’s wrong. If you put an artist in a booth and surround the booth with the players so that the artist in the booth can see those players. Certainly the drums are in the middle of the room but then the bass player and there’s a couple of guitar players and a keyboard player, you want to keep them all tight so that they all bounce off of each other. These dates where you get the guy puts the piano in another room, and the booth is in another room and the drums are in another room, you know to me my work was — it never worked because the band could never feel that they’re working with a band. I tried to always make the dates so that the guitar players could look at the drummer, the bass player could look at the — everybody had to look at each other.
